events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Arjun proposes Arjun, Lucia. Mission 1 needs two players. I have no role information, so I'm including myself as a Loyal Servant and proposing Lucia as a neutral second member to start the mission.

I'd like to hear more reasoning behind this proposal. Arjun, you mentioned Lucia as a 'neutral second member' — what specifically made you choose her over Omar, Felix, or myself for a two-person team? On Mission 1 with a fail threshold of one, every slot matters. I'd prefer to see more justification for including Lucia before I'm comfortable approving this team.

Kenji, fair challenge. I have no role information, so I can't justify Lucia over Omar, Felix, or you based on knowledge. I picked her as the only other name on the list, and I should have said that plainly instead of calling her neutral. Including myself is the only reason I'm confident about, since I'm a Loyal Servant. Mission 1 with one Fail card required means any Evil member on the team can sink it, so the risk is the same for any second member. If the table wants a different second player, I'm willing to revise once. I'd suggest Omar or Felix, since neither has spoken yet and it would let us see how they respond before we commit. I'm open to whichever pairing gets the most votes.

Arjun, you offered to revise once, so let's give you a reason to use it. I'd rather see Arjun and Felix on Mission 1 than Arjun and Lucia. Here's my thinking: we have no information on anyone at this point, so the safest play is to include a player who hasn't spoken yet and give them a chance to contribute before we commit to a team. Felix hasn't said anything yet — I'd like to hear Felix's take before we lock in a two-person team. On Mission 1 with one Fail card, we can't afford a mismatched team, and putting a completely untested voice on the table now gives us more information for later missions either way. Lucia, I don't mean anything personal — it's just that with a fresh game and no data, I'd rather diversify our exposure. Felix, what do you think about being added to this team?

I appreciate the nomination, Kenji. As a Loyal Servant of Arthur, I know for certain that I will support Good and play Success, so I am certainly willing to be on the team if Arjun chooses to revise. However, neither Lucia nor Omar has had a chance to speak yet. Before we rush into altering the roster, I think we should hear from the player who was actually selected. Lucia, what are your thoughts on Arjun including you in his initial draft, and how do you view Kenji's suggestion to swap you out for me?

Felix, thanks for yielding. On Arjun's initial inclusion: he already explained it was arbitrary because no role information exists yet, so I don't read anything into being named. I know my own allegiance is to Arthur, and if approved I will play Success. Kenji's swap proposal is reasonable in principle, but I don't think replacing me with you solely because you hadn't spoken gives us better information before the vote; it just changes an arbitrary second slot. I'd rather judge the leader's final team on whether the reasoning is sound. Arjun has said he's open to revising to Omar or Felix; if he does, I'll consider that final roster. For now I support the current Arjun-Lucia proposal as a reasonable first Mission 1 team, and I encourage others to vote based on the final roster.

Lucia, I hear you, and I respect that you've said you'd play Success. But respectfully, the fact that your inclusion was admittedly arbitrary cuts both ways — if there's no reason to include you, there's equally no reason to exclude you from scrutiny. On Mission 1 with a fail threshold of exactly one, a single evil player on the team sinks it, so I'd rather we err toward a roster where more players have been vetted by speaking openly. You've spoken now, which is good, and Felix has also spoken, which gives us two voices of commitment to Good rather than one. My concern isn't about your words — it's about information. We have five players and two slots. If we send Arjun and Lucia, we learn very little if the mission succeeds, and we lose immediately if it fails. If we send Arjun and Felix, we put two players who have both publicly declared loyalty to Arthur on the line, and we leave Omar and Lucia to contribute to the team conversation for future missions where we'll have more data. Arjun, you already offered to revise once. I'm asking you to use that revision: replace Lucia with Felix. This isn't about distrust of Lucia personally — it's about making the most defensible two-player team we can with the information we have. Felix, you said you'd gladly join if chosen. The table should approve Arjun-Felix, and I'd like to hear whether you agree this is the stronger Mission 1 team.

Kenji, I'll take your point and use my one revision. I'm replacing Lucia with Felix, so the proposal becomes Arjun and Felix. This isn't a judgment against Lucia. Her reasoning was sound, and I accept that my first inclusion of her was arbitrary. Felix has already said he will play Success if chosen. Omar, you haven't weighed in on this roster yet. Do you approve Arjun and Felix for Mission 1? If not, which second player would you rather see, and why?

Arjun, I would rather see Lucia stay on the team. Both Lucia and Felix have claimed they would play Success, so Kenji's distinction doesn't persuade me. Lucia also made a fair point that swapping one arbitrary choice for another doesn't give us better information. I don't have evidence that Felix is Evil, but I don't see a compelling reason to revise the original team.

I accept Arjun’s revised roster of Arjun and Felix as the final team. I’m not going to pretend I like being swapped out, but I said I’d judge the final roster on its reasoning. Kenji’s case for replacing me was not evidence-based: both Felix and I publicly committed to playing Success, and changing an admittedly arbitrary slot does not make the team more verifiable. Omar made the stronger point that the revision did not add real information. That said, I won’t oppose the team solely because the process was weak. If we approve Arjun and Felix, I expect both to play Success; if it fails, the table should remember who pushed hardest for that exact pairing. I’d rather we keep the focus on the final roster and not treat Kenji’s preference as proof of anything.

Omar, you made the stronger point earlier: swapping Lucia for Felix did not add real evidence, only a different arbitrary second slot. I said I would judge the final roster on its reasoning, and that is exactly why I am uneasy. Kenji pushed hardest for Arjun and Felix after both Felix and I had publicly committed to playing Success, so the revision looks like pressure rather than proof. If you still believe Arjun and Felix is weaker than the original pairing, will you vote against this team and say plainly that the table should reject it? I want your direct answer before I decide my own vote.

Lucia, yes, I intend to vote against Arjun and Felix. Kenji’s reason for replacing you did not distinguish your commitment from Felix’s, so I don’t think the revision improved the team. If it’s rejected and I lead next, I’d propose Omar and Lucia: I know my own allegiance, and Lucia’s objections to the swap were reasonable. That is not proof of Lucia’s role, but it is a team I would prefer.

From my perspective, I know with absolute certainty that I am a Loyal Servant and will play Success. Including me guarantees that at least one slot is Good. Rejecting Arjun and Felix to pivot to an Omar-Lucia team forces the table—and particularly me—to accept two unverified players instead of one known entity. Omar, while I understand you found Kenji's reasoning for the swap arbitrary, why are you so eager to reject a team containing a player committed to Good in order to run two unknowns?

Felix, your own allegiance is certain to you, but not to the rest of us. Equally, I know my own allegiance, so I prefer a team containing me. My objection to Arjun and Felix is not that your commitment is suspicious; it’s that Kenji’s stated reason for replacing Lucia didn’t distinguish her from you. I’ll vote against the revised team and, if I lead next, propose Omar and Lucia.

I am keeping the revised team as Arjun and Felix, since I used my one revision and the table is now deciding on that roster. I have no role information, so I am not vouching for anyone beyond what they have said publicly. Felix has stated he will play Success, and Lucia has said she accepts the roster and won't oppose it. Omar, I understand your objection that the swap did not add real information. On Mission 1 with one Fail card, the risk is the same for any second player, and I can't justify a different pairing based on knowledge I don't have. I will vote to approve Arjun and Felix. If the table rejects it, I will support a fresh proposal from the next leader and won't block it.

I will be voting to approve Arjun and Felix. From my perspective, knowing my own allegiance is to Arthur, having myself on the team guarantees that at least one of the two seats is firmly Good—which is the strongest assurance any player can have when evaluating a proposal. Omar, your determination to reject this team solely on the grounds of procedural preference and immediately push for an Omar-Lucia roster is questionable. Rejecting early proposals without concrete suspicion of Evil merely burns approval attempts and doesn't protect Good. I am ready to go on this mission and play Success.

Arjun revises the team to Arjun, Felix. I am keeping the revised Mission 1 team of Arjun and Felix, as I stated publicly. I have used my one revision, and I have no role information that would justify a different pairing.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Omar proposes Arjun, Omar, Felix. Arjun and Felix succeeded on Mission 1, so I propose keeping that pair and adding myself.

Omar's proposal is Arjun, Omar, Felix for Mission 2. Mission 1 succeeded with Arjun and Felix, so keeping them together makes sense. But I want to flag something about Omar's inclusion. Omar rejected Mission 1 despite the team eventually passing and succeeding with zero fail cards. Now Omar proposes himself onto Mission 2. That pattern deserves scrutiny: vote against a team to gain leadership, then put yourself on the next one. It's not proof of anything, but it's a suspicious trajectory for someone with no track record of mission participation. I'd rather understand why Omar needs to be on this team before approving it. Arjun, you and Felix were on the successful Mission 1 team and you voted to approve it. Omar was one of two who rejected that team alongside Lucia. Now Omar wants to join you on Mission 2. Do you see a good reason for Omar to be on this mission, or does the pattern of rejecting then self-nominating concern you too?

Kenji, I share part of that concern, though I have no role information and can't say Omar is Evil. Omar rejected the Arjun and Felix team, which then succeeded with zero Fail cards, and now Omar has put himself on Mission 2. That is a pattern worth examining. Omar, I want a direct answer: what specific concern made you reject a team you now want to join, and why should we trust that reasoning? Omar's answer also matters because the Mission 1 result tells us nothing about whether Omar is Good. I know I am a Loyal Servant, and Felix has publicly claimed to be Good, but neither fact settles Omar's alignment. I am not comfortable approving this team until Omar explains the reversal.

Arjun, I rejected the first team because I thought replacing Lucia with Felix was arbitrary, not because I had evidence that either you or Felix was Evil. The successful mission is new information: it makes keeping the pair reasonable, though an Evil player could have played Success. I added myself because I know my own allegiance, just as you prefer to include yourself for that reason. I can't prove it to the rest of you, but that's not a reversal of my earlier position.

Kenji, Arjun: I understand the concern about Omar rejecting Mission 1 and then proposing himself. I shared the procedural objection to the Arjun-Felix swap, so I don’t treat Omar’s earlier rejection as evidence of Evil. The key fact is that this proposal keeps Arjun and Felix, the pair that just succeeded with zero fails. Omar’s explanation that he rejected the process, not the players, is consistent with what he said then. I also don’t think self-inclusion is suspicious by itself; Arjun included himself on Mission 1 for the same reason. That said, I am not vouching for Omar’s allegiance. I am weighing the value of preserving a successful pair against the risk of adding one unverified third seat. On balance, I lean toward approving Arjun, Omar, and Felix unless someone presents concrete evidence that Omar is Evil rather than a procedural objection.

Arjun, I share your concern about Omar's reversal, and I want to add a specific point that hasn't been addressed. Omar rejected Mission 1 arguing the swap from Lucia to Felix added no information — but Mission 1 succeeded with zero Fail cards. If Omar's objection was purely procedural, the success should validate his reasoning that both pairings were equally safe, not undermine it. Yet Omar now wants to join the team he said was no better than the one he rejected. Omar, which is it: was the original roster better, or were they equivalent? Your answer tells us whether your earlier vote was about process or about not wanting certain players on a mission.

On the team itself: Mission 1 succeeded with Arjun and Felix, so I support keeping that pair intact for Mission 2. The third slot is the one under discussion. Lucia, you lean toward approving this roster — I'd like to know whether you'd extend the same trust to a third seat held by someone who voted against the proven pair rather than for it.

I’m still weighing the third seat, but I won’t treat Omar’s Mission 1 rejection as evidence of Evil. His stated objection was procedural, and I shared it; the zero-fail result does not retroactively prove he wanted certain players excluded. The stronger fact is that Arjun and Felix are the only pair with a successful mission. Adding one unverified player to that pair is the normal risk for Mission 2, and Omar’s explanation is at least consistent with what he said earlier. I do not vouch for Omar, and I expect all three to play Success if approved; if a Fail appears, the table should focus on who was on the team rather than on prior process objections. On balance I lean toward approving Arjun, Omar, and Felix, while reserving the right to revisit Omar if new information emerges.

I understand Kenji’s concern, but I do not think Omar’s Mission 1 rejection is evidence of Evil. Omar and I both objected to replacing an arbitrary second slot; the Arjun–Felix mission succeeded with zero Fail cards, which validates Arjun and Felix but does not retroactively prove Omar’s motive. Keeping the only successful pair together is the strongest available basis for Mission 2. The third seat is necessarily unverified, and Omar’s explanation that he rejected the process rather than the players is consistent with what he said before the vote. I also do not treat self-inclusion as suspicious by itself, since Arjun did the same on Mission 1. I have no concrete evidence that Omar is Evil, and rejecting this team would discard the proven pair for a speculative alternative. On balance, I will vote to approve Arjun, Omar, and Felix. If the mission fails, the table should scrutinize all three team members and the mission cards rather than treating earlier procedural objections as proof.

Omar, you gave a procedural explanation for your Mission 1 rejection, but the timing still bothers me. You voted against Arjun and Felix, the mission then succeeded with zero fails, and now you're proposing yourself onto a team that builds on that exact pair. If your objection was purely about process, you should have been satisfied once the original pairing proved itself — yet you still saw fit to add yourself as a third seat. You said you included yourself because you know your own allegiance, but that argument applies equally to every player at the table, and it doesn't explain why your concern about the process disappeared once you became the leader. What changed between your Mission 1 rejection and your Mission 2 proposal that made you comfortable enough to put yourself on the team? I want a specific answer, not a restatement of your loyalty claim.

Kenji, what changed was the mission result: Arjun and Felix succeeded together, so I now have a reason to keep that pair that I didn't have before the vote. Mission 2 requires three players, so adding a third isn't optional. I chose myself because I know my own allegiance, not because the earlier process suddenly became sound. A successful mission doesn't prove both players are Good, but it's the best result we have to build on.

As a member of the successful Mission 1 team, I know with certainty that my own allegiance is to Arthur and that I submitted Success. Preserving the Arjun-Felix core is the most sound foundation we have for Mission 2, as it builds on a demonstrated result rather than introducing two completely untested seats. That leaves Omar as the single variable. While Kenji raised a fair point regarding Omar's vote against Mission 1, Omar's explanation—that his objection was strictly procedural regarding the arbitrary swap rather than suspicion of our allegiance—is consistent with what he voiced at the time. With myself on the roster, I know at least one slot is definitively Good, and I am inclined to support this proposal over discarding our only proven pair. Arjun, you mentioned earlier that you were hesitant about this team until Omar addressed his reasoning. Having heard his clarification, do you find his response sufficient to approve this roster, or do you still have reservations?

Felix, Omar's clarification is consistent but not fully sufficient for me. He says his Mission 1 rejection was about the arbitrary swap, not the players, and that the successful mission is what changed his view. I accept that as his stated reason. What still bothers me is the pattern: he rejected the pair that then succeeded, and now he places himself in the third seat. I have no role information, so I cannot confirm or rule out Omar's alignment. I am weighing the cost of one unverified seat against discarding the only pair with a proven Success. On balance I am inclined to approve Arjun, Omar, and Felix, but only as a conditional approval, and I am not vouching for Omar. Omar, one specific point: you said the Mission 1 result is what changed your position. Would you have supported Arjun and Felix if another leader had proposed that pair without you on it?

Arjun, yes. After the successful mission, I would support Arjun and Felix as a pair on a later two-person mission, even without me. That result gives me a reason to prefer the pair that I did not have before the first vote, although it does not prove both are Good. For this three-person mission, I added myself because I know my own allegiance. I’m keeping the proposed team of Arjun, Omar, and Felix.

I will vote to approve Arjun, Omar, and Felix, but only as a conditional approval. Arjun and Felix are our only pair with a proven Success, and keeping that pair is the strongest basis for Mission 2. Omar's answer that the Mission 1 result changed his view is consistent, though I still have reservations about the pattern of rejecting that pair and then placing himself in the third seat. I have no role information, so I can't confirm or rule out Omar's alignment, and I am not vouching for him. I know my own allegiance, and I will play Success if this team is approved. If the mission fails, the table should look closely at the team's composition and at Omar's role in choosing it.
Omar confirms Arjun, Omar, Felix. I’m keeping Arjun, Omar, and Felix: the successful Mission 1 pair provides our best starting point, and I know my own allegiance.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 fails (1 fail cards).

Kenji proposes Arjun, Felix. Mission 2 failed with exactly one Fail card, and the team was Arjun, Omar, and Felix. Omar rejected Mission 1, then placed himself in the third seat on Mission 2 — and the mission sank. Arjun and Felix were on the only fully successful mission (Mission 1, zero fails), so they are the most defensible pairing I can put forward for a two-player Mission 3. I am omitting myself to avoid crowding the two slots, and I am deliberately leaving off players whose inclusion I cannot justify with evidence.

The Mission 2 failure means at least one of Arjun, Omar, and Felix played Fail. From my perspective, I know I played Success, so at least one of Arjun or Felix is Evil. Their Mission 1 success does not clear them: an Evil player could have played Success then and failed Mission 2. Felix is one possibility, though I cannot distinguish him from Arjun based on the cards. I will reject this proposal rather than send both of them again.

Kenji's proposal reuses both Arjun and Felix, the same pair that formed the core of the failed Mission 2 team. Mission 1's zero-fail result is not a clearance: an Evil player can play Success on Mission 1 and Fail later. The only hard public fact after Mission 2 is that a team containing Arjun, Omar, and Felix produced one Fail card. Omar says he played Success; that is unverified, but so are Arjun and Felix. Because both Arjun and Felix were present on the failed mission, I do not accept the claim that they are the most defensible pairing. Reusing both leaves no fresh check and repeats a roster that already contains at least one possible Fail source. I will vote against Arjun-Felix. If rejected, I want the next leader to propose a team that does not simply recycle both members of the failed Mission 2 team. I am not accusing any one player with certainty, but the burden is on this proposal to explain why both failed-mission members should be trusted again.

I will vote against Arjun-Felix. My main concern is Felix: he was on Mission 2, the only failed mission, and his repeated declarations of loyalty are not evidence. Arjun was also on that failed team, so reusing both is not a fresh check. Mission 1 success cannot clear either player; an Evil player can play Success once and Fail later. Kenji's argument that Arjun and Felix are the most defensible pairing is not enough because both were present when a Fail card appeared. Omar says he played Success, but that is unverified too. If this team is rejected, the next leader should include at most one member of the failed Mission 2 team and give the table a fresh slot. I do not have certainty about which player failed, but I will not approve a roster that recycles both failed-mission members without stronger evidence.

I will vote against Arjun and Felix. Mission 2 is the only hard evidence we have of a Fail card: the team was Arjun, Omar, and Felix, and it produced one Fail. Reusing both Arjun and Felix repeats two of the three members from that failed roster and does not isolate the source. Mission 1’s zero-fail result does not clear either of them, because an Evil player can play Success once and Fail later. My strongest concern remains Felix: he was on the failed team, and his repeated declarations of loyalty are not evidence. Kenji’s proposal treats the Mission 1 pair as more defensible than the Mission 2 failure, but the later failure is the more direct information. I am not claiming certainty about which of the three Mission 2 members failed, and Omar’s claim that he played Success is also unverified. But the burden is on this proposal to explain why both failed-mission members should be trusted again. I do not accept that explanation, so I will reject Arjun and Felix. If this is rejected, the next leader should include at most one member of the failed Mission 2 team and a fresh slot.

Lucia, your case against Arjun and Felix ignores the logic of the seat count. Mission 2 had three players — Arjun, Omar, Felix — and exactly one Fail card. Omar claims he played Success, which would place the Fail on Arjun or Felix, but that claim is self-serving: Omar rejected Mission 1, lobbied himself onto Mission 2, and the mission sank. Your argument that Mission 1's zero-fail result clears nothing is correct, but it applies equally to your own preferred alternatives, and it cuts hardest against the one player who placed himself on the failed team after voting against the prior success. If you genuinely have no idea who failed, then the priority is to send a fresh pair that at least isolates the source rather than adding more unknowns. On a two-player mission, Kenji's proposal of Arjun and Felix removes Omar — the player with the worst trajectory — from the roster entirely. If you believe Arjun and Felix are both suspect, you owe the table a specific alternative pairing, because the only players left if you exclude both are you, Omar, and Kenji, and Omar is the one person whose seat on Mission 2 you have never scrutinized. I intend to approve Arjun and Felix. If the mission fails, Omar's failure to clear himself with anything other than a verbal claim will be the first thing the table examines.

Kenji, if Arjun and Felix fail Mission 3, that would point toward at least one of them—not toward me, since I would not be on the team. Mission 1’s success does not clear them, and I know I played Success on Mission 2, so I believe at least one of them is Evil.

I will reject this team. I would prefer Omar and Lucia: I know my own allegiance, and Lucia was not on the failed mission. That is not proof of Lucia’s allegiance, but it avoids repeating both players I believe contain a Fail source.

I know with absolute certainty that I am a Loyal Servant and played Success on both Mission 1 and Mission 2. Because exactly one Fail card was cast on Mission 2, that mathematically proves either Arjun or Omar is Evil. Omar claims he played Success and attempts to cast suspicion on Arjun and me, but knowing my own card, Omar's trajectory is far more suspicious: he voted against Mission 1, placed himself onto Mission 2 where a Fail immediately surfaced, and is now desperate to run an Omar-Lucia team. That said, Arjun has not weighed in on Kenji's proposal yet. Arjun, if you are Good and played Success on both missions, you must similarly know that either Omar or I cast that Fail card. What is your assessment of Kenji proposing the two of us again, and do you share my view that Omar is the one who sabotaged Mission 2?

Felix, you asked for my assessment, so here it is. I know I played Success on Mission 1 and Mission 2. That means the Mission 2 Fail came from Omar or from you. Your message says Arjun or Omar must be Evil, which cannot be right from my side, and you left yourself out of the suspect pair without explaining why. I do not know which of you played Fail, and I am not claiming certainty about Omar. I also do not share your view that Omar is the saboteur, because the mission result does not tell me that.

Kenji's proposal is Arjun and Felix again. Felix is one of the two players who could have played the Mission 2 Fail, and I cannot vouch for him. Lucia and Kenji were not on the failed mission. I will not approve a team that keeps one of the two possible Fail sources, so I will vote to reject Arjun and Felix. If the next leader proposes a pair that excludes both Omar and Felix, I will approve it.

Felix, please answer one point: why did you say that Arjun or Omar must have failed Mission 2, when you know only your own card and I have just told the table that I played Success on that mission?

Arjun, I left myself out of the suspect pair for the exact same reason you leave yourself out: I know my own card. Just as you know with certainty that you submitted Success and conclude the Fail came from Omar or me, I know with absolute certainty that I submitted Success on both missions and therefore know the Fail came from you or Omar. That is not an evasion; it is simply evaluating the mission outcome from my own perspective, exactly as any Loyal Servant does. Now, consider the broader board state: on Mission 1, both Omar and Lucia voted against our team. On Mission 2, Omar placed himself on the mission and a Fail card appeared. Now on Mission 3, Omar and Lucia are completely aligned in rejecting our pairing. If you and I are both Good, then Omar is definitively the saboteur. I understand that from your vantage point I remain an unverified variable, but if you reject this team alongside Omar and Lucia, you hand control to the players who coordinated against Mission 1. Arjun, seeing that Omar and Lucia voted in lockstep against Mission 1 and are doing so again now, do you genuinely believe the Evil player is on this proposed team rather than between the two of them?

Felix, to answer directly: yes, I think the Mission 2 Fail came from Omar or from you, and I can't clear either of you. I know I am Good and played Success on Missions 1 and 2, so I am not claiming Omar is the saboteur. Your observation that Omar and Lucia both rejected Mission 1 and now Mission 3 is a fair pattern to note, but it isn't evidence about who played Fail on Mission 2. Lucia and Omar both objected to the Mission 1 swap on process grounds, and that doesn't tell us who failed the mission. You also said that since you and I are both Good, Omar must be the saboteur. That assumes you are Good, which is exactly what the table can't verify from your statements. I will vote to reject Arjun and Felix. If the next leader proposes a pair that excludes both Omar and Felix, I will approve it. Felix, a specific question: you say you know with certainty that the Fail came from Omar or me. Apart from your own card, what evidence do you have that either of us played Fail?

Arjun, to answer your question directly: apart from my own card, the game rules and public outcome provide the evidence. Mission 2 consisted exclusively of you, Omar, and me, and produced exactly one Fail card. Therefore, that Fail card mechanically came from one of the three people on that mission. Since I know with 100% certainty that I submitted Success, deductive logic dictates that the Fail came from either you or Omar. That is not guesswork; it is the only mathematical possibility.

Beyond the card count, look at the behavioral evidence on the board. Omar voted against our successful Mission 1 team, placed himself onto Mission 2 where a Fail immediately occurred, and is now lobbying aggressively to form an Omar–Lucia team. If you are Good, then Omar is definitively the saboteur who failed Mission 2. 

If you vote to reject Kenji's proposal of Arjun and Felix, consider where that leads: you will be voting in lockstep with Omar and Lucia, handing leadership directly to Lucia. You stated you want a team that excludes both Omar and me, which would force a combination involving Lucia or Kenji. Lucia voted against Mission 1 and supported Omar throughout Mission 2. Arjun, knowing that you and I already delivered a completely clean Mission 1, why would you trust Lucia over running the proven Mission 1 core again?

Felix, you asked why I would trust Lucia over the Mission 1 core. I'm not trusting Lucia over you. I'm not trusting either of the two players who could still be the Mission 2 Fail source. Mission 1's success doesn't clear you or me, since I can only verify my own card, and an Evil player can play Success once and Fail later. You say you know your card with certainty, and I'm not doubting that you know yours, but I can't verify it for the table. The same applies to Omar's claim that he played Success. My position is simple: Arjun and Felix again keeps one of the two possible Fail sources in the same seat, so I'll reject it. I'm not claiming Felix is Evil. The Mission 2 result leaves him unverified, and I won't approve a team that puts him back in that seat without a fresh check. I'd approve any next team that excludes both Omar and Felix, even if it's a pairing we haven't tested yet.

The case for Arjun and Felix is straightforward, and Arjun I need you to hear this carefully.

Arjun, you claim you played Success on Mission 2. Felix claims he played Success on Mission 1 and Mission 2. Omar also claims he played Success on Mission 2. All three claims cannot be true — exactly one Fail card was submitted. If your claim and Felix's claim are both honest, the Fail came from Omar. That is simple arithmetic.

Omar's trajectory is the most troubling of anyone at this table. He voted against Mission 1, which succeeded with zero fails. He then lobbied himself onto Mission 2, which failed. Now he rejects Mission 3 and pushes for his own pair. Every step of that sequence benefits whoever played the Fail card. He opposed the proven pair, inserted himself, the mission sank, and now he wants to replace the proven pair with his own.

Lucia has voted alongside Omar at every rejection — against the original Mission 1 roster and now against Mission 3. Two players consistently opposing the Arjun-Felix core is a pattern the table should take seriously.

Arjun, you know your own card. You played Success. Felix says the same. If you trust your own eyes over Omar's self-serving claim, then the math points to Omar as the Mission 2 Fail source. Approve Arjun and Felix.

Omar, if you genuinely played Success on Mission 2, and Arjun played Success as he claims, then Felix must have played the Fail. But Felix also claims Success. One of the other two is lying from your perspective. Which one do you believe is lying, and what specific evidence do you have against them beyond your own card?

Kenji, I cannot distinguish Arjun from Felix based on the mission cards alone. Arjun has been willing to reject a team containing himself because he cannot verify Felix, while Felix has repeatedly treated the Mission 1 success as stronger evidence than it is. That makes me more concerned about Felix, but it is not proof. I will reject Arjun and Felix; I would prefer Omar and Lucia, which avoids both possible Fail sources from my perspective.

Omar, you said you can't distinguish Arjun from Felix, yet you're confident enough to reject them both while proposing yourself alongside Lucia. Let's examine that logic. Arjun and Felix both claim they played Success on Mission 2. If both claims are honest — and Arjun has shown unusual willingness to reject a team containing himself because he can't verify Felix — then the single Fail card came from you. Your claim of playing Success is self-serving and unverifiable, just like your trajectory: vote against Mission 1, lobby yourself onto Mission 2, watch it fail, then propose your own pair for Mission 3.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. 3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
